facts.text: Miston’s post office opened in 1909, marking its formal recognition amid growing agricultural networks.
The community sits on low‑lying floodplains about 272 feet above sea level, a feature that shapes its fertile loess‑derived soils.
Miston developed in the mid‑19th century as a small farming enclave, sometimes called “Baggett‑ville,” after the Civil War’s agricultural expansion.
Located just 5 miles east of the Mississippi River, Miston’s proximity once allowed farmers to ship cotton by steamboat.
The town lies along Tennessee State Route 103, 3 miles east of Bogota and 13 miles northwest of Dyersburg, placing it near the county’s western edge.
Miston’s climate is humid subtropical, with July highs around 90°F and annual rainfall about 53 inches, typical of West Tennessee lowlands.
